title: What the jury in the Lindsay Clancy trial is deliberating | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

The Massachusetts jury in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial resumed deliberations Monday as they debated questions around reasonable doubt, criminal responsibility and mental illness.

Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse, haspleaded not guiltyin the killings of her children Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months.

Both the prosecution and defense agree Clancy fatally strangled her children with exercise resistance bands on January 24, 2023. To secure a murder conviction, prosecutors have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt she intentionally caused their deaths and is “criminally responsible.”

Judge William Sullivan explained the legal meaning of criminal responsibility to the jury at the start of the trial:

““A person is not criminally responsible for her conduct if she has a mental disease or defect, and as a result of that mental disease or defect, lacks the substantial capacity either to appreciate the criminality or the wrongfulness of her conduct or to conform her conduct to the requirements of the law.””

Under Massachusetts law, a “mental disease or defect” does not need to fit into a formal medical diagnosis. Both sides agree Clancy had postpartum mental health issues beginning in September 2022.

Prosecutors have argued she still had the capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness of her actions and could follow the law. They pointed out she sent herhusband out to run errandsbefore killing the kids, and upon waking in a hospital, sheasked for an attorney.

“I’m not saying she was happy about it. I’m saying, it was what she had to do to end her misery,” prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said in closing arguments. “But it was a choice. It was a choice.”

However, the defense has argued she killed them during an episode of postpartum psychosis. They cited Clancy’s declining mental health in the months beforehand and her statements afterward thatshe heard a persistent male voicecommanding her to kill her children and herself.

“It was almost like she was a puppet and someone else was pulling the strings,” Dr. Phillip Resnick, a forensic psychiatrist, testified for the defense during the trial.

The trial has put a renewed spotlight onmaternal mental healthand prompted a group of pink-wearing women to rally outside court in a show of support for and sympathy with Clancy.

The jury is considering five potential verdicts: guilty of first-degree murder, guilty of second-degree murder, guilty of manslaughter charges, not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility and not guilty.

First-degree murder means she killed the children with “deliberate premeditation” or with “extreme atrocity or cruelty,” and is punishable by life in prison without parole. Second-degree murder has neither condition and is punishable by life in prison with the possibility of parole.

Manslaughter means she intentionally acted with “wanton or reckless conduct” that resulted in her children’s deaths and is punishable by up to 20 years in prison.

If the jury finds prosecutors have not proven Clancy was criminally responsible, she would be found not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility. In that case, the court may begin the process of committing her to a mental health facility.

Finally, the jury can consider a simple not guilty verdict if they determine the prosecution did not prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt.

Per Massachusettsstate law, when a person is found not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility, a court can commit them to a facility after holding a hearing and determining if they are mentally ill and if their release would create a likelihood of serious harm to themself or others. An initial commitment lasts six months, and later commitments last one year.

There is no maximum number of re-commitments, and the patient could remain hospitalized for the rest of their life.

Clancy, who is partially paralyzed, has been held at Tewksbury Hospital since 2023. She continues to take several medications for her mental health issues and remains on the highest level of suicide precautions, according to testimony from psychologist Dr. Kirk Heilbrun.

“What it says to me is she was at risk for suicide, (and) she remains at risk for suicide. She still is,” he said.

CNN’s Nicki Brown contributed to this report.

CNN’s Nicki Brown contributed to this report.
